scope: Seven current installed Start Smarter lesson videos, selected from index.html; Welcome has no standard LESSON_VIDEOS entry. Local-file review, not a public-site verification.
method: Full sequential decode of all seven files; fresh timestamped automatic transcripts read in full; full-duration visual sampling every six seconds; selected opportunities inspected at one-second intervals. These are frame-and-transcript findings, not continuous audiovisual playback or a shipping certification. Proposed windows need frame-level and audible alignment before production. Automatic transcripts can contain recognition errors.
recommendation: Pilot three moments in two videos: show a patient tutor in use, make the phone-prediction analogy concrete, and show active recall after the study instructions. Keep the other five videos as they are for this first batch. The first two are the clearest gains; the third tests whether a short action scene strengthens the study takeaway.

opportunities.title: Show the patient tutor in use
opportunities.cue: 0:29.26–0:38.24: “It will happily quiz you at one in the morning. It never sighs when you ask it to explain a concept for the fifth time, and it meets you exactly where you are stuck.”
opportunities.current: Two small comparison/process diagrams show availability and a pinned problem step. Their headings include “Infinite Patience & Exact Diagnostics,” and a label assigns an emotional state to AI. They explain the claim in abstract terms without showing a student asking for help.
opportunities.proposal: A realistic high-school student at a home desk in warm lamplight, with an attempted algebra problem on paper. The student asks the AI to explain the step they are stuck on. Keep the paper attempt, the specific help request, and the response area visible together. One composed scene, with a simple screen reveal if needed.
opportunities.benefit: Makes “ask again” and “where you are stuck” observable actions. The picture gives students a model for asking for targeted help, without adding a claim that the tool always diagnoses perfectly or has feelings.
opportunities.treatment: Replace only the two supporting diagrams in this window. Use photographic realism matching Why Learn AI?, ordinary student clothing, natural proportions, and a restrained push only if the paper and screen stay readable. Add essential screen text deterministically; do not rely on generated microtext. Preserve the following desk scene and tool-choice introduction.
opportunities.board: No canonical board affected. No new rings, pauses, or narration.
opportunities.success: At 720p, a viewer can identify what the student has tried and what help they ask for. The student remains the one doing the work.

opportunities.title: Make the phone analogy visible
opportunities.cue: 3:41.89–3:50.31: “This diagram shows a process similar to the predictive text keyboard on your phone. It suggests a word, you tap it, and it suggests the next.”
opportunities.current: A small animated predict/select/update loop generates “The sky…” while the narration describes tapping suggestions on a phone. The loop is useful, but the familiar phone action itself is absent.
opportunities.proposal: A close photographic view of a phone at a student's desk, with a clean, precisely rendered predictive keyboard. Use the lesson's peanut-butter phrase: tap “jelly,” append it, then show the next suggestions. The screen is the subject; the hand and desk provide context.
opportunities.benefit: Connects an abstract repeated prediction process to an action the student recognizes. It shows that choosing a word changes the text used for the next suggestion.
opportunities.treatment: Begin at the supporting-diagram entrance, after the probability-board takeaway. Use a short controlled screen animation rather than a motionless phone photograph. Return to the existing loop at “But a language model continuously loops…” around 3:51, then retain the One Word at a Time board and the later paragraph-building animation. Final boundaries are provisional.
opportunities.board: Preserve Same Word. Different Odds. and One Word at a Time, including their current highlights and camera paths. Change only the intervening supporting shot.
opportunities.success: The tap, added word, and updated suggestions are readable as three events. It remains clear that the phone analogy involves a human tap while the LLM continues automatically.

opportunities.title: End with the learner doing the work
opportunities.cue: 3:21.56–3:28.38: “Executing these four moves stops you from passively reading summaries and forces you to actively test and strengthen your memory.”
opportunities.current: The full Four Moves board returns and holds its takeaway highlight. The exact quiz prompt has already been read while its card remains on screen at 3:03–3:09.44.
opportunities.proposal: Reuse the tutor scene's student and setting. Show a quiz question with its answer hidden, the student recording an answer from memory, and then a restrained feedback reveal. Keep any reference notes closed or face down so the retrieval action is unmistakable.
opportunities.benefit: Shows what active recall looks like, turning the closing advice into a behavior a student can repeat. Reusing the scene creates continuity between getting help and testing yourself.
opportunities.treatment: Keep the full board visible through the start of the four-moves summary, then insert roughly 3:23–3:29.83 and cut directly to the existing standard close. Use two or three clear screen states within one stable composition. If the three actions feel rushed, show question plus student answer only, or omit this addition; do not extend the audio or runtime.
opportunities.board: Your Four Moves for Gemini Notebook: preserve the full opening, all four complete-card views and highlights, and the citation drawing. Keep the exact quiz prompt on screen for its entire spoken reading. Only shorten the final full-board takeaway hold; preserve its initial exposure and the unchanged close.
opportunities.success: The viewer sees that the learner must answer before feedback appears. The scene must work in under seven seconds without speeding through a mini tutorial.

opportunities.title: A personal response to music
opportunities.cue: 2:43.70–2:51.74 contrasts a person's emotional response to art or music with AI describing beauty using learned patterns.
opportunities.current: The comparison board highlights the Beauty row for the full explanation. The distinction is already explicit and readable.
opportunities.proposal: A short photographic paired scene: a teenager responding to a school performance, alongside a clear example of a text description of that performance. Use a simple label for each role if needed.
opportunities.benefit: Could make an abstract distinction memorable, but the picture must show both experience and description. A smiling student alone would add little.
opportunities.treatment: Defer until after the pilot. Keep the Beauty row visible at its introduction and return for Uncertainty. Preserve the existing fact-checking student around 2:57–3:02 and the owner-requested continuous Chinese Room walkthrough.
opportunities.board: When You Think. What AI Does.: possible short Beauty-row cutaway only; other rows unchanged.
opportunities.success: The paired scene communicates the distinction more quickly than the current readable row. Otherwise leave the current version.

opportunities.title: Show one tangible generated output
opportunities.cue: 1:20.42–1:27.50 lists an email, essay, image, website, song, and video as possible outputs.
opportunities.current: An animated hub progressively reveals those output categories. The earlier prompt-to-patterns sequence and later superhero example already explain creation.
opportunities.proposal: If the pilot shows a benefit, briefly show a plausible student-made club website or poster next to the AI request that produced its first draft. Keep the output large enough to recognize.
opportunities.benefit: Adds a tangible end product, but one example sacrifices the existing overview of six formats. This is a lower-priority tradeoff, not a needed repair.
opportunities.treatment: Default to retaining the current animation. Do not replace the recommendation selection animation or the superhero comparison. Consider a cutaway only if it aligns with the named output and avoids rapid montage.
opportunities.success: The draft visibly answers the request; a generic laptop scene is insufficient.

lessons.title: Why Learn AI?
lessons.reason: The navigation screen (1:10.30–1:13.30), chatbot student (1:31.80–1:37.30), and project-feedback student (2:48.20–2:53.20) each show a specific narrated action. Preserve the printing-press and desktop-publishing sequences too. No additions proposed.

lessons.title: What Is AI?
lessons.reason: Keep the desk hook, recommendation-selection example around 1:03–1:08, prompt-to-output reveals around 1:15–1:27, and superhero comparison. The existing motion carries relationships; photographic uniformity alone would not improve them.

lessons.title: How an LLM Works
lessons.reason: Add the phone action at the spoken analogy. Retain the training walkthrough (about 0:46–1:44), context/probability comparison, token caveat, word-by-word board, and paragraph loop around 4:27–4:43.

lessons.title: Does AI Think?
lessons.reason: Keep the Chinese Room's coherent step-by-step walk, including the owner-requested uninterrupted 1:09.50–1:50.17 span. Keep the literal-rulebook-versus-learned-patterns sequence around 1:51–2:07 and the existing realistic fact-checking student near 3:00.

lessons.title: In Your Hands
lessons.reason: The installed v6 already has realistic scenes of the same student testing, planning, and building a club-events app. Five cutaways occur at 1:18, 1:41, 2:09, 2:23, and 2:37. Adding more similar scenes has no established learning benefit.

lessons.title: Beyond the New Average
lessons.reason: Keep the shared-tool/common-starting-point progression (0:15–0:43), knowledge-and-skills comparison (1:00.6–1:09.5), school container reveal (1:09.5–1:17.4), and concrete writing/building/teamwork scenes. One-second inspection confirms meaningful state changes; replacing these with stills would lose explanatory structure. This also respects the prior scene-by-scene reassessment.

lessons.title: Learn with AI
lessons.reason: Add targeted help in use and a short active-recall action. Keep the tool-choice comparison, uploads-to-study-tools sequence, exact quiz prompt, and citation-to-source drawing around 3:17–3:21. The current four-move instructions should remain readable.
